t.1.213.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When all the Vṛṣṇis had spoken their words again and again, then Vāsudeva spoke words endowed with dharma and artha.
t.1.213.2: Guḍākeśa has offered no insult to this family; rather, without doubt, he has shown it a surpassing honour.
t.1.213.4: Who would consent to the giving away of a maiden as though she were an animal? And what man on earth would sell his own offspring?
t.1.213.3: Pārtha never regards you Sātvatas as greedy for wealth, and the Pāṇḍava also considers a svayaṃvara to be something not to be ventured upon.
t.1.213.5: It is my belief that the son of Kuntī saw these faults; therefore the Pāṇḍava carried off the maiden by force, in accordance with dharma.
t.1.213.6: The alliance is indeed a fitting one, and Subhadrā is illustrious; and this Pārtha, being such as he is, has carried her off by force, so he reasoned.
t.1.213.9: Such indeed is that chariot, and those horses are mine, and the warrior is Pārtha, swift with his weapons; who, then, could be equal to him?
t.1.213.7: Who would not wish to have Arjuna, born in the lineage of Bharata and of the great-souled Śaṃtanu, the son of Kuntibhoja's daughter?
t.1.213.10: Pursue Dhanaṃjaya and, rejoicing, turn him back with the most conciliatory words; this is my highest counsel.
t.1.213.11: If Pārtha were to defeat you by force and go to his own city, your glory would perish at once; but in conciliation there is no defeat.
t.1.213.8: And I see no one, O worthy one, who could defeat Pārtha by valour, even in all the worlds together with Indra and the Rudras.
t.1.213.12: Having heard those words of Vāsudeva, they did as he said, O lord of men. Arjuna returned there and then celebrated the marriage.
t.1.213.13: Having dwelt there for nights exceeding a year, the mighty son of Kuntī then spent the remaining time at the Puṣkaras; and when the twelfth year was complete, he entered Khāṇḍavaprastha.
t.1.213.14: Having approached the king with humility, composed and attentive, and having honored the brāhmaṇas, Pārtha went to Draupadī.
t.1.213.15: Draupadī, out of affection, replied to that delight of the Kurus: "Go right there, Kaunteya, where that daughter of the Sātvatas is; even when a burden is tightly bound, the first binding grows slack."
t.1.213.17: And Pārtha, in haste, sent Subhadrā on ahead, clad in red silk, after she had taken on the appearance of a cowherd girl.
t.1.213.16: As Kṛṣṇā lamented thus in many ways, Dhanaṃjaya consoled her, and again and again he begged her forgiveness.
t.1.213.18: Shining all the more in that form, the glorious lady, the hero's wife, that most excellent of women, reached the finest of dwellings, and the illustrious Bhadrā, with her large copper-tinged eyes, paid homage to Pṛthā.
t.1.213.20: Kṛṣṇā rose and embraced her, the sister of Mādhava, and, pleased, said, "May your husband be without a rival wife!" Bhadrā, delighted in the same way, said to her, "So be it."
t.1.213.19: Then Bhadrā, whose face was like the full moon, quickly approached and paid homage to Draupadī, and said, "I am your servant."
t.1.213.21: Then those great chariot-warriors, the sons of Pāṇḍu, were glad at heart, and Kuntī too became supremely delighted, O Janamejaya.
t.1.213.24: Surrounded by his brothers, by the young princes, and by warriors in their hundreds, and protected by a great army, came Śauri, the scorcher of foes.
t.1.213.26: Anādhṛṣṭi of great splendor, and Uddhava of great fame, a direct disciple of Bṛhaspati himself, of great intellect and great renown.
t.1.213.25: There came the wise and greatly renowned Akrūra, lord of generosity, the tamer of foes and commander of the army of the Vṛṣṇi heroes.
t.1.213.23: Keśava, pure of soul, came together with Rāma, accompanied by the chief ministers of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas and by heroic great chariot-warriors.
t.1.213.22: But then the lotus-eyed one heard that Arjuna, best of the Pāṇḍavas, had reached his own excellent city and was now in Indraprastha.
t.1.213.28: And the valiant Cārudeṣṇa, and Jhillī and Vipṛthu too, and the mighty-armed Sāraṇa, and Gada, foremost among the learned.
t.1.213.27: Satyaka and Sātyaki, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata, Pradyumna and Sāmba, Niśaṭha and Śaṅku as well.
t.1.213.29: These and many others as well, Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas and Andhakas, came to Khāṇḍavaprastha, bringing abundant wedding gifts.
t.1.213.30: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard that Mādhava had arrived, sent forth the twins at that time to receive Kṛṣṇa.
t.1.213.31: Received at the hands of those two, that prosperous host of the Vṛṣṇis, resplendent with banners and standards, entered Khāṇḍavaprastha.
t.1.213.32: It had its roads sprinkled and swept clean, was adorned with strewn masses of flowers, and was perfumed with cool juices of sandalwood of holy fragrance.
t.1.213.33: It was fragrant with sweet-smelling aloewood burning here and there, well swept and thronged with people, and adorned with merchants.
t.1.213.35: Being honored by the townspeople and by brāhmaṇas in their thousands, he entered the palace of the king, which resembled the abode of Puraṃdara.
t.1.213.34: The mighty-armed Keśava, the supreme among men, arrived together with Rāma, surrounded by the great Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas and Bhojas.
t.1.213.36: Yudhiṣṭhira met with Rāma in accordance with custom, and, kissing Keśava on the head, embraced him with his arm.
t.1.213.38: And Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of dharma, received those foremost of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas with honors, according to rule and as each one approached.
t.1.213.37: Kṛṣṇa, for his part, humbly honored him, who was filled with delight, and in return he duly honored Bhīma, the tiger among men.
t.1.213.39: Some he honored as elders, some as friends; some he greeted with affection, and by some he was himself saluted.
t.1.213.40: Then the greatly famed Vāsudeva gave, for the sake of the bridal party, the most excellent wealth as the wedding gift of Subhadrā, the gift that is to be given by the kinsmen.
t.1.213.41: Kṛṣṇa gave a thousand chariots with golden fittings, garlanded with networks of little bells, each yoked with four horses and furnished with charioteers esteemed for their skill, and ten thousand cows as well.
t.1.213.42: The glorious Janārdana, out of affection, gave a thousand gold-adorned milch cows from the land of Mathurā, of pure radiance, and a thousand white mares whose splendor equalled the rays of the moon.
t.1.213.43: Likewise he gave tamed she-mules, swift as the wind: five hundred with manes black as collyrium, and five hundred white ones.
t.1.213.44: And a thousand fair-complexioned women, beautifully dressed and radiant, endowed with youth and well skilled in bathing and anointing.
t.1.213.45: The lotus-eyed one bestowed women who wore necklaces of a hundred gold pieces, free from illness, beautifully dressed, and skilled in every kind of service.
t.1.213.47: Of elephants in rut, exuding ichor from three places, resembling mountain peaks, never turning back in battles.
t.1.213.46: Janārdana, the Dāśārha, gave ten man-loads of the finest gold, both worked and unworked, gleaming with the radiance of fire.
t.1.213.48: He who delights in daring deeds gave a thousand excellent elephants, well equipped, with shrill-sounding bells and golden garlands, each furnished with its riders.
t.1.213.49: Rāma, the plough-bearer, the wielder of the plough, gave Pārtha the gift for the clasping of the feet; delighted, he brought about the joy of their new kinship.
t.1.213.52: Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of dharma, accepted all of it, and he also honored those great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
t.1.213.50: That flood of great riches and jewels, foaming with garments and blankets, had mighty elephants for its great crocodiles and was thick with banners as with water-weed.
t.1.213.51: Like a great surging river it poured into the ocean of the Pāṇḍus, and, filling what was already full, it brought grief to their enemies.
t.1.213.53: Those great-souled ones, the foremost of the Kurus, Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, having come together, sported and took their pleasure, just as men of virtuous deeds do in the abode of the immortals.
t.1.213.54: Here and there, with great drinking bouts resounding with loud hand-clapping, the Kurus and Vṛṣṇis amused themselves as suited each occasion and as each one pleased.
t.1.213.55: Thus those men of supreme valour, having enjoyed themselves for many days and been honoured by the Kurus, went back again to the city of Dvāravatī.
t.1.213.56: Placing Rāma at their head, the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas departed, taking with them the splendid jewels given by the best of the Kurus.
t.1.213.57: But the high-minded Vāsudeva dwelt right there with Pārtha, O Bhārata, in the delightful city of Śakraprastha; and he roamed along the bank of the Yamunā together with Pārtha, O Bhārata.
t.1.213.59: Subhadrā gave birth to the hero Abhimanyu, a bull among men, long-armed, of great courage, with eyes like a bull's, a tamer of foes.
t.1.213.60: Because he was fearless and full of fiery spirit, they therefore called that crusher of foes, the son of Arjuna and bull among men, Abhimanyu.
t.1.213.61: That great chariot-warrior was born of Dhanaṃjaya in Sātvatī, as fire, the eater of oblations, springs forth at a sacrifice from the śamī wood as it is churned.
t.1.213.58: Then Subhadrā, the beloved sister of Keśava, gave birth to the radiant Saubhadra, as Paulomī gave birth to Jayanta.
t.1.213.62: When he was born, the mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, gave ten thousand cows to the twice-born, and as many gold coins.
t.1.213.63: From his very childhood he was dear to Vāsudeva and to all his fathers, as the moon is dear to all creatures.
t.1.213.64: From his very birth Kṛṣṇa performed the auspicious rites for him, and the boy grew like the moon in the bright fortnight.
t.1.213.65: The tamer of foes learned from Arjuna, knower of the Vedas, the entire science of archery, with its four parts and ten divisions, both divine and human.
t.1.213.67: Dhanaṃjaya made his son Saubhadra equal to himself, as it were, in learning and in practice, and gazing upon him, he was delighted.
t.1.213.66: The mighty one taught him the finer points in the knowledge of weapons, in skill and dexterity, and in all the practical techniques as well.
t.1.213.68: Him, endowed with every bodily excellence and marked with all the auspicious signs, unassailable, with shoulders like a bull's, like a serpent with gaping jaws.
t.1.213.71: And Pāñcālī too, she of auspicious marks, obtained from her five husbands five heroic, splendid sons, like five mountains.
t.1.213.70: Bībhatsu beheld his son, the equal of Kṛṣṇa in valor, in prowess, in beauty and in form, just as Maghavan had once beheld him.
t.1.213.69: Him who had the pride of a lion, a great archer with the valor of a rutting elephant, whose voice resounded like thunderclouds and kettledrums, and whose face shone like the full moon.
t.1.213.73: From Sahadeva she bore Śrutasena; these five heroes, great chariot-warriors, Pāñcālī brought forth, as Aditi bore the Ādityas.
t.1.213.72: She bore Prativindhya to Yudhiṣṭhira, Sutasoma to Vṛkodara, Śrutakarman to Arjuna, and Śatānīka, the son of Nakula.
t.1.213.75: When a thousand Soma sacrifices had been performed, she bore to Bhīmasena Sutasoma, the great archer, whose splendour equalled that of the moon and the sun.
t.1.213.74: In accordance with the śāstra, the brahmins told Yudhiṣṭhira that the boy was Prativindhya, saying, “In the knowledge of the weapons of enemies, let this one be Prativindhya.”
t.1.213.77: Nakula, the Kauravya, the joy of the Kurus, gave his son, the increaser of fame, the same name as the royal sage Śatānīka.
t.1.213.76: When Kirīṭin had returned after accomplishing a great and renowned deed, he was told, “A son has been born to you”; thus the boy came to be called Śrutakarman.
t.1.213.79: And the illustrious sons of Draupadī were born one after another, each a year apart, O king of kings, devoted to one another's welfare.
t.1.213.78: Then Kṛṣṇā bore to Sahadeva a son under the constellation whose deity is Fire; therefore they know him as Śrutasena.
t.1.213.80: O best of the Bharatas, Dhaumya duly performed for them, in proper order, the birth rites, the tonsure ceremonies and the sacred-thread initiations.
t.1.213.81: Having completed the study of the Vedas, they, faithful in keeping their vows, then learned from Arjuna the whole science of arrows and weapons, both divine and human.
t.1.213.82: Accompanied by their sons, who were like the offspring of gods, broad-chested and of great strength, the Pāṇḍavas, O tiger among kings, attained joy.
